title: Must you wipe the whole head in wudu?

summary.text: The four schools disagree on how much of the head must be wiped in wudu: the Malikis and Hanbalis hold that the whole head must be wiped, while the Hanafis and Shafi'is hold that wiping part of it discharges the obligation. All of them agree that wiping the head is obligatory in wudu and that covering the whole head is better.

paragraphs.text: The command comes in the verse of wudu, which includes the words "wipe over your heads" (Quran 5:6). The dispute turns on the preposition bi in bi ru'usikum: Ibn Rushd frames it as whoever took the ba as redundant or confirmatory required the whole head, and whoever took it as partitive required only part. Ibn Qudama rejects the partitive reading, arguing the ba here is for contact, so the sense is "wipe your heads," which covers all of it.

The same verse supplies a second argument: its tayammum clause says "wipe your faces and hands," and the face must be covered completely in tayammum. Ibn Abd al-Barr reports Ibn Ulayya reasoning that since partial washing of the face is not accepted in wudu and partial wiping of it is not accepted in tayammum, the head in wudu must likewise be taken whole. Al-Bukhari himself titled a chapter in his Sahih "Wiping the entire head, based on the saying of Allah: 'And wipe your heads'".

Companion practice was not uniform: Ibn Umar used to wipe only the crown of his head with one pass, and Ibn Abi Shayba recorded with sound chains that he wiped the front of his head once. Salama ibn al-Akwa' and Uthman are also reported wiping the front of the head only. When Malik was asked whether wiping part of the head suffices, he argued back from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd.

The strongest report describes the Prophet ﷺ wiping his head with his hands, moving them forward and backward, beginning at the front of his head, taking his hands to the back of his neck, then bringing them back until he returned to the place where he had begun (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 32). At-Tirmidhi grades it sahih, al-Albani sahih, and Zubair Ali Zai marks it agreed upon; the Ahmad route is judged sound on the condition of the two Shaykhs.

The report used by the part-view is al-Mughira's: the Prophet performed ablution and passed a wet hand on his forelock, over the turban, and over the two leather socks (Sahih Muslim 274k). A second wording says he wiped "the front part of his head, and over his turban", and it is sahih. Related reports have him wiping over the turban alone, graded sahih in Tirmidhi, with the Ahmad route weak in chain but sound through other routes.

Al-Rubayyi' bint Mu'awwidh reported that the Prophet wiped his head, the front and back of it, his temples and his ears once; at-Tirmidhi said this is a hasan sahih hadith. Abdullah bin Zaid saw the Prophet wipe his head with water other than what was left on his hands; at-Tirmidhi said this is a hasan sahih hadith. Ali wiped his head once, as did Uthman and Salamah ibn al-Akwa'.

The statement "the ears are part of the head" is hasan in Tirmidhi, though the narrator Hammad admitted he did not know whether it was the Prophet's ﷺ words or Abu Umamah's; the Ahmad route of it is graded da'if jiddan.

The Hanafis require a quarter of the head, wiped with at least three fingers, as stated in al-Marghinani's al-Hidaya and Ibn Abidin's Radd al-Muhtar. Al-Marghinani opens his chapter by deriving the obligations straight from the verse, listing washing the three limbs and wiping the head. Ibn Abidin explains that the quarter is established by probable evidence rather than decisive proof, which is why it is called a "practical" obligation: wipe a single hair instead and validity is lost. Ibn Rushd notes that Abu Hanifa also fixed the wiping hand at no less than three fingers.

The Malikis require the whole head, as in Malik's al-Mudawwana and Ibn Rushd's Bidayat al-Mujtahid. In the Mudawwana, Malik says a woman wipes her whole head even if her hair is braided, and does not wipe over her khimar. Ibn Rushd adds that some of Malik's own companions set the minimum at a third or two-thirds.

The Shafi'is hold that any part suffices, down to part of a single hair, as in al-Shirbini's Mughni al-Muhtaj. Al-Shirbini argues from al-Mughira's hadith that sufficing with part is what the report shows, and that since no one holds the forelock specifically obligatory, sufficing with it, which is less than a quarter, rules out both full coverage and a fixed quarter minimum. A Shafi'i fatwa spells out the minimum: resting the hand on the head without moving it, dripping water without letting it flow, or washing the head.

The Hanbalis require the whole head, with a second report from Ahmad that part suffices, as in Ibn Qudama's al-Mughni and al-Buhuti's Kashshaf al-Qina'. Ibn Qudama states there is no disagreement that wiping the head is obligatory, then reports Ahmad's view that the whole head is required, calling it the apparent position of al-Khiraqi and the madhhab of Malik; he also reports Ahmad saying of a man who left part of his head, "it suffices him," and remarking, "who is able to cover the entire head?". Al-Buhuti writes that however one wipes it, it suffices, even with one finger, a cloth or a stick, while the apparent view of the majority is that the whole outer head must be covered, with some excusing a small omission out of hardship.

The main reconciliation is over al-Mughira's hadith. Ibn al-Qayyim states that not a single sound hadith shows the Prophet ﷺ restricting himself to part of his head at all; whenever he wiped the forelock he completed the wiping over the turban. Ibn Uthaymeen makes the same point, saying the forelock sufficed there only because the turban was wiped with it. Al-Buhuti applies this to the report of wiping the front of the head, reading it as done together with the turban as al-Mughira's hadith explains.

The grammatical dispute is met by denying the partitive ba. Ibn Qudama's reply is that the ba is for contact, giving the sense of the whole head, and the tayammum parallel is then used to close the case. The Shafi'i reply in Mughni al-Muhtaj cuts the other way, treating the forelock as proof that full coverage is not required and that no fixed fraction was legislated.

On practice, the "whole head" position does not mean separate wipes for every patch: one pass in the Prophetic manner, front to nape and back, achieves it, which is why the answer warns against treating it as waswas. The two descriptions of the wipe, hands returning to the front for short hair and a single downward pass for long hair that would otherwise tangle, are both reported from him.

The Permanent Committee's fatwa collection states that the obligatory act is wiping all of the head, citing the verse and the Bukhari–Muslim report of Abdullah ibn Zayd. Ibn Baz was asked directly whether wiping part suffices and answered that the whole head must be wiped, following the Prophet's ﷺ practice; in another answer he told a woman taught that wiping was only a sunnah done from the front that she must repent and wipe from the front to the back near the neck, though past prayers need not be repeated.

Ibn Uthaymeen held the same: the verse means the whole head, and wiping only the forehead is invalid unless one is wearing a turban, in which case the exposed part is wiped along with the turban. Al-Albani also concluded that the whole head is required and found nothing in al-Shawkani's argument to support a quarter. IslamQA's two answers reach the same conclusion, calling full coverage the weightier view.

From the Hanafi side, SeekersGuidance answers that one need not wipe every hair, that a quarter of the head is the obligation, and that wiping the whole head once is the emphasised sunnah. Egypt's Dar al-Ifta presents the disagreement and notes that the Hanafi position in the school's relied-upon view is that a quarter is the obligatory amount, while covering the whole head from front to nape and back is recommended.
